title: Finding the Maximum in Each Sliding Window

phrases.explanation: A technique where a fixed-size subset moves across the data one step at a time
A straightforward approach that checks every possibility without optimization
A measure of how the running time grows as input size increases
An unusual or extreme input that may cause unexpected behavior
A sequence where each element is less than or equal to the one before it

technical_terms.definition: A double-ended queue that supports insertion and removal from both front and back in constant time
A deque maintained so that elements are always in sorted order, either increasing or decreasing
A subarray of fixed length k that shifts one position to the right at each step
The average time per operation over a sequence of operations, even if some individual operations are costly
Storing indices instead of values to track both position and value of elements

java_methods.description: Creates a double-ended queue backed by a resizable array
Returns the element at the front of the deque without removing it
Returns the element at the back of the deque without removing it
Removes and returns the element at the front of the deque
Adds an element to the back of the deque

concept: Given an integer array and a window size k, slide a window of size k from left to right across the array. For each window position, find the maximum element. Return an array of all such maximums.

solutions.label: Brute Force Scan
solutions.summary: For each window position, scan all k elements to find the maximum.

solutions.label: Max-Heap Approach
solutions.summary: Use a max-heap to track the current window's maximum, removing expired elements lazily.

solutions.label: Monotonic Deque
solutions.summary: Maintain a decreasing deque of indices so the front always holds the current window's maximum.

sections.title: Understanding the Problem
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["Array: 1, 3, -1, -3, 5, 3, 6, 7"] --> B["Window k = 3"]
    B --> C["Position 1: [1, 3, -1] → max 3"]
    B --> D["Position 2: [3, -1, -3] → max 3"]
    B --> E["Position 3: [-1, -3, 5] → max 5"]
    B --> F["Position 4: [-3, 5, 3] → max 5"]
    B --> G["Position 5: [5, 3, 6] → max 6"]

    style A fill:#f87171
    style B fill:#f87171

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Here's the problem. You're given an integer array and a number k. Imagine a window of size k sliding from the left end of the array to the right, one element at a time. At each position, you need to report the maximum value inside that window.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Got it. So for example, with the array one, three, negative one, negative three, five, three, six, seven and k equals three, the first window holds one, three, negative one, giving a max of three. Then the window shifts right, and I repeat. Is that correct?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Exactly. A few constraints: the array length can be up to a hundred thousand, and k is always between one and the array length. Elements can be negative.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: What if k equals one? Then each element is its own window, so the output is just the original array. And if k equals the array length, we return a single-element array with the overall maximum. Are those right?

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Yes, both are correct. The output array will always have exactly n minus k plus one elements. Please return an integer array.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Understood. So I need to slide a window of size k across the array and collect the maximum of each window into a result array of size n minus k plus one. Let me start with a straightforward approach.

sections.title: Brute Force Scan
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["Window 1: [1, 3, -1]"] -->|scan all 3| B["max = 3"]
    C["Window 2: [3, -1, -3]"] -->|scan all 3| D["max = 3"]
    E["Window 3: [-1, -3, 5]"] -->|scan all 3| F["max = 5"]
    G["Window 4: [-3, 5, 3]"] -->|scan all 3| H["max = 5"]
    I["Window 5: [5, 3, 6]"] -->|scan all 3| J["max = 6"]
    K["Window 6: [3, 6, 7]"] -->|scan all 3| L["max = 7"]
    style A fill:#60a5fa
    style C fill:#60a5fa
    style E fill:#60a5fa
    style G fill:#60a5fa
    style I fill:#60a5fa
    style K fill:#60a5fa

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The simplest idea is to loop through each window starting position from index zero to n minus k. For each position, I scan all k elements to find the maximum and store it in the result.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Walk me through the cost of that approach.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: There are about n minus k windows, and each window scan takes O of k time. So overall it's O of n times k. Space is O of one, ignoring the output array. When k is large, say close to n, this becomes O of n-squared, which is too slow for a hundred thousand elements.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Right. The repeated scanning is the bottleneck. Can you think of a way to avoid rescanning the entire window each time?

sections.title: Max-Heap Approach
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["Add 1, 3, -1 to heap"] --> B["Heap top = 3 → output 3"]
    B --> C["Add -3, heap top = 3 → output 3"]
    C --> D["Add 5, heap top = 5 → output 5"]
    D --> E["Add 3, heap top = 5 → output 5"]
    E --> F["Add 6, heap top = 6 → output 6"]
    F --> G["Add 7, heap top = 7 → output 7"]
    style A fill:#a78bfa
    style B fill:#a78bfa
    style D fill:#a78bfa
    style F fill:#a78bfa

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: I can use a max-heap. I add each element along with its index. The heap's top always gives the largest value. Before recording the max, I check if the top element's index is still within the current window. If it's expired, I pop it and check the next one.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: What's the time complexity of that?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Each insert and removal is O of log k. We insert n elements total, so it's O of n log k. That's much better than n times k. Space is O of k for the heap. However, in the worst case, stale elements can pile up, though they get cleaned lazily.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Good improvement. Can we do even better than O of n log k?

sections.title: Monotonic Deque
sections.diagram:
graph TD
    A["i=0: deque [0] → val 1"] --> B["i=1: 3 > 1, pop 0, deque [1]"]
    B --> C["i=2: -1 < 3, deque [1,2] → output max=3"]
    C --> D["i=3: -3 < -1, deque [1,2,3] → output max=3"]
    D --> E["i=4: 5 > all, clear, deque [4] → output max=5"]
    E --> F["i=5: 3 < 5, deque [4,5] → output max=5"]
    F --> G["i=6: 6 > 3 and > 5, deque [6] → output max=6"]
    G --> H["i=7: 7 > 6, deque [7] → output max=7"]
    style A fill:#fb923c
    style C fill:#fb923c
    style E fill:#fb923c
    style G fill:#fb923c

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: The key insight is a monotonic deque. I store indices in a deque, keeping it in decreasing order of their values. When I add a new element, I remove all indices from the back whose values are smaller, since they can never be a window maximum while the new element is present.

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Let me trace through our example. At index zero, I push zero. At index one, value three is greater than one, so I pop zero and push one. At index two, negative one is smaller than three, so I just push two. The deque holds indices one and two. The front is index one with value three, which is our first output.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: How do you handle elements leaving the window?

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: Before recording each answer, I check if the front index is outside the window, meaning it's less than i minus k plus one. If so, I remove it from the front. Each element enters and leaves the deque at most once, so the total work is O of n. Space is O of k for the deque.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Excellent. That's optimal. Let's wrap up with a comparison.

sections.title: Summary
sections.diagram:
graph LR
    A["Brute Force
O of n times k
O of 1"] --- B["Max-Heap
O of n log k
O of k"]
    B --- C["Monotonic Deque
O of n
O of k"]
    style A fill:#60a5fa
    style B fill:#a78bfa
    style C fill:#fb923c

lines.speaker: candidate
lines.text: To summarize, the brute force scans each window in O of n times k. The max-heap improves this to O of n log k by avoiding full rescans. The monotonic deque achieves O of n by ensuring each element is processed at most twice, once entering and once leaving the deque.

lines.speaker: interviewer
lines.text: Great breakdown. The monotonic deque is a powerful pattern. Whenever you need to efficiently track a maximum or minimum in a sliding window, this technique gives you linear time. Well done.
